{{Short description|Geological process relating to earthquakes}}
'''Coulomb stress transfer''' is a [[Seismology|seismic]]-related [[geology|geological]] process of [[Stress (mechanics)|stress]] changes to surrounding material caused by local discrete deformation events.<ref name="one">{{cite journal|last=King|first=G.C.P. |author2=Stein, R.S. |author3=Lin, J.|title=Static stress changes and the triggering of earthquakes|journal=Bulletin of the Seismological Society of America|year=1994|volume=84|issue=3|pages=935–953}}</ref> Using mapped displacements of the Earth's surface during [[earthquake]]s, the computed Coulomb stress changes suggest that the stress relieved during an earthquake not only dissipates but can also move up and down [[Fault (geology)|fault]] segments, concentrating and promoting subsequent tremors.<ref name="two">{{cite journal|last=Stein|first=R.S.|authorlink=Ross Stein|title=Earthquake Conversations|journal=Scientific American|year=2003|volume=288|issue=1|pages=72–79|doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0103-72|pmid=12506427 |bibcode=2003SciAm.288a..72S}}</ref> Importantly, Coulomb stress changes have been applied to earthquake-forecasting models that have been used to assess potential [[Seismic hazard|hazards]] related to earthquake activity.<ref name="one" /><ref name="two" /><ref name="three">{{cite journal|last=Stein|first=R.S. |author2=Barka, A.A. |author3=Dieterich, J.H.|title=Progressive failure on the north Anatolian fault since 1939 by earthquake stress triggering|journal=Geophysical Journal International|year=1997|volume=128|issue=3 |pages=594–604|doi=10.1111/j.1365-246x.1997.tb05321.x|bibcode = 1997GeoJI.128..594S |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="four">{{cite journal|last=Barka|first=A.A.|author2=Rockwell, T. K. |author3=Reilinger, R. |author4=Imren, C. |title=Kinematics of the central marmara sea ridges|journal=Eos, Transactions, American Geophysical Union|year=1999|volume=80|issue=46|page=664}}</ref><ref name="five">{{cite journal|last=Parsons|first=T.E.|author2=Dreger, D.S.|title=Static-stress impact of the 1992 landers earthquake sequence on nucleation and slip at the site of the 1999 M = 7.1 hector mine earthquake, southern California|journal=Geophysical Research Letters|year=2000|volume=27|issue=13|pages=1949–1952|doi=10.1029/1999gl011272|bibcode = 2000GeoRL..27.1949P |s2cid=49218075 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Coulomb stress change==

The [[Mohr–Coulomb theory|Coulomb failure criterion]] requires that the Coulomb stress exceeds a value σ<sub>f</sub> defined by the [[shear stress]] τ<sub>B</sub>, [[normal stress]] σ<sub>B</sub>, [[pore pressure]] p, and [[coefficient of friction]] μ of a failure plane, such that

<div class="center" style="width: auto; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">{{bigmath| σ<sub>f</sub> {{=}} τ<sub>B</sub> – μ(σ<sub>B</sub> – p) }}<ref name="one" /></div>

It is also often assumed that changes in pore fluid pressure induced by changes in stress are proportional to the normal stress change across the [[Fault (geology)|fault]] plane.<ref name="six">{{cite journal|last=Beeler|first=N.M. |author2=Simpson, R. W., J. |author3=Hickman, S. H. |author4=Lockner, D. A. |title=Pore fluid pressure, apparent friction, and coulomb failure|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research|year=2000|volume=105|issue=25|page=542|doi=10.1029/2000JB900119|bibcode = 2000JGR...10525533B |s2cid=4685444 |url=http://digitalcommons.unl.edu/usgsstaffpub/412 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> These effects are incorporated into an effective coefficient of friction μ’, such that

<div class="center" style="width: auto; margin-left: auto; margin-right: auto;">{{bigmath| Δσ<sub>f</sub> {{=}} Δτ<sub>B</sub> – μ’(Δσ<sub>B</sub>)}} <ref name="six"/></div>

This simplification allows for the calculation of Coulomb stress changes on a fault plane to be independent of the regional stress field but instead depends on the fault geometry, sense of slip, and coefficient of friction.

The significance of the Coulomb stress changes was discovered when mapped displacements of neighbouring [[Fault (geology)|fault]] movements were used to calculate Coulomb stress changes along faults. Results revealed that the stress relieved on faults during [[earthquake]]s did not simply dissipate, but also moved up and down fault segments. Moreover, mapped lobes of increased and decreased Coulomb stress around local faults exhibited increased and decreased rates of seismicity respectively shortly after neighboring earthquakes, but eventually return to their background rate over time.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Dieterick|first=J.H.|author2=Kilgore, B.D.|title=Direct observation of frictional contacts; new insights for state-dependent properties|journal=Pure and Applied Geophysics|year=1994|volume=143|issue=1–3|pages=283–302|doi=10.1007/bf00874332|bibcode = 1994PApGe.143..283D |citeseerx=10.1.1.494.3198|s2cid=129103586 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Toda|first=S.|author2=Stein, R.S.|title=Toggling of seismicity by the 1997 Kagoshima earthquake couplet; a demonstration of time-dependent stress transfer|journal=Journal of Geophysical Research|year=2003|volume=108|issue=B12|page=12|doi=10.1029/2003jb002527|bibcode = 2003JGRB..108.2567T |citeseerx=10.1.1.459.2321}}</ref>

==Earthquake stress triggering==
{{see also|Remotely triggered earthquakes}}

Stress triggering describes the responsive rupturing of [[Fault (geology)|faults]] from increases in Coulomb stress caused by [[wikt:exogenous|exogenous]] deformation events.<ref name="one"/> Although neighboring displacements often yield small magnitude stress changes, areas of disturbed Coulomb stress states have been successfully used to explain the spatial distribution of stress triggered aftershock [[seismicity]].

On June 28, 1992, a [[1992 Landers earthquake|M7.3 earthquake]] that struck near [[Landers, California]], was followed (about three hours later) by the [[1992 Big Bear earthquake|M6.5 Big Bear foreshock]] earthquake 40&nbsp;km away. Calculated Coulomb stress changes from both of these earthquakes showed a westward lobe of 2.1–2.9 bars of increased Coulomb stress to have resulted from the displacement associated with both earthquakes. Of the roughly 20,000 [[aftershock]]s that occurred 25 days after June 28 within a 5&nbsp;km radius, more than 75% occurred in areas where Coulomb stress had increased and less than 25% occurred in areas where Coulomb stress had dropped.<ref name="one"/>

Another successful case study of earthquake prediction occurred along Turkey's [[North Anatolian fault]] system. From 1939 to 1999, the Anatolian fault system had witnessed ten earthquakes of M6.6 or greater. The evolution of the Coulomb stress changes along the North Anatolian fault as a result of these earthquakes showed that 11 of the 13 ruptures occurred in areas of increased Coulomb stress caused by a previous rupture.<ref name="three"/><ref name="four"/> This method has been also used to predict seismicity around active volcanoes submitted to significant variation of stress in the magma chamber.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=J.Gargani |author2=L.Geoffroy. |author3=S.Gac, S.Cravoisier |title=Fault slip and Coulomb stress variations around a pressured magma reservoir : consequences on seismicity and magma intrusion|journal=Terra Nova|year=2006|volume=18|issue=6 |pages=403–411|doi=10.1111/j.1365-3121.2006.00705.x|bibcode=2006TeNov..18..403G|s2cid=128537724 }}</ref>

==Earthquake prediction==
{{main|Earthquake prediction}}

Although no official Coulomb stress transfer prediction model is being used by government agencies, geologic surveys often analyze [[earthquake]] threats using Coulomb stress theory. As an example, the last of the previous thirteen earthquakes along Turkey's [[North Anatolian Fault]], near the town of Duzce, was successfully predicted by local geologists before the rupture occurred. This allowed for engineers to evacuate unstable structures and limit significant damage.<ref name="two"/> Scientists estimate that the probability of another earthquake along the Anatolian fault system is 62% over the next 30 years and will be located threateningly close to Istanbul.<ref name="three"/>

==Examples of earthquake sequences==
*[[1703 Apennine earthquakes]]
*[[1761 Lisbon earthquake]] – located on a fault under the [[Coral Patch Seamount]] adjacent to the location of the [[1755 Lisbon earthquake]]
*[[1783 Calabrian earthquakes]]
*[[1899 Yakutat Bay earthquakes]]
*[[1981 Dawu earthquake]] – part of a sequence of four along the [[Xianshuihe fault system]]<ref name="Zhang">{{cite journal|last=Zhang|first=Q. |author2=Zhang P. |author3=Wang C. |author4=Wang Y.  |author5=Ellis M.A.|year=2003|title=Earthquake triggering and delaying caused by fault interaction on Xianshuihe fault belt, southwestern China|journal=Acta Seismologica Sinica|volume=16|issue=2|pages=156–165|bibcode = 2003AcSSn..16..156Z |doi = 10.1007/s11589-003-0018-5 |s2cid=128487233 }}</ref>
*[[2001 Gujarat earthquake]] – fault reactivation caused by built-up stress from the [[1819 Rann of Kutch earthquake]] 
*[[2005 Nias–Simeulue earthquake]] – triggered by the [[2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami|2004 Indian Ocean earthquake]] 3 months prior
*[[2007 Kuril Islands earthquake]] – [[Normal fault|normal faulting]] from an [[Outer trench swell|outer rise]] area next to where the [[2006 Kuril Islands earthquake]] nucleated
*[[2012 Indian Ocean earthquakes]]
*[[2018 Sulawesi earthquake and tsunami|2018 Sulawesi earthquake]] – inferred to have been related to the [[1996 Sulawesi earthquake]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lei |first=Dongning |last2=Wu |first2=Jianchao |last3=Yang |first3=Gang |date=2020 |title=Coseismic Coulomb stress changes imparted by the 1996 Minahasa Mw7.9 earthquake on the 2018 Palu Mw7.5 earthquake and expected seismicity rate changes |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ter.12434 |journal=Terra Nova |language=en |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=44–52 |doi=10.1111/ter.12434 |issn=1365-3121|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
*[[2023 Turkey–Syria earthquakes]]
*[[2026 Kumamoto earthquake]] – caused by the [[2016 Kumamoto earthquakes]] that happened to the northeast
